newsitem.title: USA: MG's Cerro deal creates copper powerhouse.
newsitem.headline: MG's Cerro deal creates copper powerhouse.

text.p: Metallgesellchaft's swift move to snap up Cerro Sales Corp in the United States for an undisclosed price has stunned rivals and created a powerhouse in physical copper trading, dealers said.
But there is also some concern that once Cerro comes under the wing of MG subsidiary MG Metal & Commodity Group, COMEX copper futures turnover will dwindle.
This would come as a blow to COMEX just when the exchange is trying to build up liquidity to compete against London Metal Exchange.
MG said in New York it was unable to comment on the deal announced earlier Wednesday.
Rival brokers declined to comment publicly.
"This was a bolt out of the blue and caught everyone on the hop," a broker said. "A lot of copper will now be in strong hands, merchantwise."

Cerro, part of privately held Marmon Group, is a big player in arbitrage trading, but many in the industry believe MG, which also trades the arb but to a lesser extent, is buying Cerro for its healthy physical copper customer base in the U.S., an asset MG does not have to the same extent, dealers said.
"This could steal some liquidity from COMEX and it would not go to LME," the broker said.
All physical copper trades in the U.S. are priced against COMEX.

A merchant added, "They both traded the arb and it will definitely take liquidity off COMEX. A lot of times they would be counterparties and when you put everything in one book, there will be less trading."
Others see the merger as further polarization in the U.S. physical metal industry as producers and consumers squeeze out middlemen.
"I was a bit shocked by this and it does have the potential to reduce liquidity and reduce competition. I think they will be a very powerful team," a producer-linked sales executive said.
Though some observe that because Cerro and MG often played off against each other in the market, it made them look bigger than they really were.

Nevertheless, MG and Cerro combined would be far ahead of the U.S. red metal pack, with only Glencore International, Gerald Metals, and Brandeis, part of France's Pechiney SA PECH.PA "on the same page", dealers said.
The trader pecking order was highlighted in the recent U.S. Mint tender for copper when only Gerald, MG and Cerro took part.

"I think this will create a vacuum at the start because Cerro and MG countered each other, doing opposite things in the market," a merchant said. "There is going to be, for a short while, some liquidity problems on COMEX."

Employees at Cerro were said to be unclear as to how the merger will translate into staffing and market strategies, with details of the deal still being worked out by closure scheduled for next month.
Despite any market void created by the merger, some think others will step up to the plate, as in the wake of the Sumitomo scandal, though LME volumes are still sharply down since the debacle.
"But they miss something that was never real," a broker added.
